data.title: Justice Department clears NextEra-Dominion merger
data.description:
The Justice Department (DOJ) on Thursday greenlit the merger between energy companies NextEra and Dominion, after noting concerns about the deal’s impact on electricity costs.

The DOJ said in a release the Internal Market Monitor of ISO New England, who oversees that region’s electric power system, submitted comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) — tasked with approving the NextEra-Dominion merger.

Those comments, the DOJ noted, warned the deal “might give the merged firm the incentive and ability to deactivate” an electricity plant that is “still economically viable.”

The combined entity would do so to “increase capacity payments” in the New England region, the Internal Market Monitor claimed.

Dominion and NextEra announced the nearly $67 billion merger in May, in a deal the two companies said would create the world’s largest regulated electric utility business by market capitalization. The companies said in May they anticipated closing in 12 to 18 months.

To alleviate the Internal Market Monitor’s concerns to FERC, the companies granted the regulator the authority to investigate “any plant that the merged firm proposes to deactivate” for five years starting in May 2028, the DOJ stated. 

Under the agreement, the Internal Market Monitor could bar Florida-based NextEra from deactivating a plant it determines to still have “economic value.”

Given that, the DOJ’s Antitrust Division closed its probe into the merger. The Federal Trade Commission can also raise antitrust concerns about mergers.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) in October called for the combined NextEra-Dominion entity to halt electricity rate hikes for six years if the deal goes through. Dominion is headquartered in Richmond, Va.

The Virginia State Corporation Commission must also approve the merger before the two sides can complete. Opening arguments in the state regulator’s legal review of the deal took place on Tuesday.

Rising utility bills posed a political issue for the GOP this midterm cycle, as Democrats swept to clinch control of Congress and nabbed a majority of governor’s mansions for the first time in 16 years.

Electricity prices increased by by 0.9 percent from September to October, the highest monthly increase since April, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.

data.title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
data.description:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.

And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.

The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee’s failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.

Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.

Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years “knowing the love of the father.” Then he told the warden: “Go, warden!”

Almost immediately he exclaimed: “The pain! Go! Go!” He uttered an expletive and implored “the father” to “take this pain.” “Let me go, father,” he said again and again. “Let me go. … I’m here. I’ve been your son all these years.”

Then he shouted: “My right leg is killing me!” and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, “I don’t think this is normal. Take me, father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”

After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.

The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.

Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes’ left foot and on the left side of his neck.

She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state’s procedures.

Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.

Asked if he was faking, she replied, “I think, yeah, there were allegations. … There was nothing abnormal on our part.”

“This isn’t the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It’s also not the first time we’ve had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately,” Hernandez said.

Witness Janice Copeland’s husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.

“David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right,” she said Thursday. “Finally after 30 years, justice has been served.”

Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.

Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple’s home and attacking them, saying, “I never killed anyone.”

Florida has now carried out more than half the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.

Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.

The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

Florida husband and wife were strangled

In Florida, Overton was strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.

“I’ve never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone,” Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors’ home or gated community. “I didn’t kill the MacIvors.”

The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared him dead.

The MacIvors’ bodies were found in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state’s database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors’ home.

Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.

Michael MacIvor’s sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man’s sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.

“One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive,” Sharon MacIvor said. “Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him.”

Diamonds missing in jeweler’s killing were never recovered

Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting.

Records showed she also distracted the security guard, David Copeland, at Dennes’ request. Copeland, who was shot twice, identified Dennes as his assailant.

Police found the jeweler’s body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.

Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.

A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

data.title: State lawmakers file bills to repeal Texas' bans on DEI in public schools, higher education
data.description:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — Two bills filed Wednesday by Texas Rep. Nichole Collier, D-Fort Worth, would roll back the state’s ban on what state law defines as “diversity, equity, and inclusion,” or DEI, offices at public schools and universities.

Texas implemented a ban on college DEI offices in 2024, after the passage of Senate Bill 17 during the 2023 legislative session, where it had been a priority of then-Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick. It shut down on-campus centers for minority groups and stripped funding from student groups.

Collier’s House Bill 1230 is a straight-forward repeal of that law. It has a companion in the Texas Senate, SB 125. There’s also HB 358, filed by Democratic State Rep. John Bucy III, which is effecitvely identical to HB 1230.

Texas’ public universities have complied with the ban, according to the State Auditor’s Office.

On the other side of the aisle, State Rep. Harrison, R-Midlothian, filed HB 836, which would prohibit any state agency from taking actions that promote “in whole or part” DEI. It mirrors an executive order issued by Gov. Greg Abbott in 2025.

As for public schools and open-enrollment charter schools, the Texas legislature passed a ban on DEI policies and activities in 2025’s SB 12. Collier’s HB 1233 would repeal that ban while keeping most of SB 12’s other provisions intact.

SB 12 is currently the subject of ongoing litigation in federal court. That case was brought in August by the nonprofit LGBTQ+ youth organization GSA Network, filing on behalf of students in the Houston, Katy and Plano independent school districts.

The plaintiffs and defendant school districts filed a motion to pause the case Monday.

“Voters elected a new Attorney General, who takes office on January 1, 2027. The Office of the Attorney General represents the State in this action,” the filing says. “The State is the only party defending the constitutionality of SB 12 on the merits.”

The joint motion to stay can be read below:

1116 motion to stay GSA Network v ISDsDownload

Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson recently told KXAN that he intends to review the state’s ongoing cases when he takes office. His predecessor, Ken Paxton, issued an anti-DEI legal opinion in January of this year.

The 90th Texas Legislative Session begins Jan. 12, 2027.

data.title: Europe cannot get its industrial base in order
data.description:
At the June 2025 Hague Summit, America’s NATO allies committed themselves to spending 3.5  percent of Gross Domestic Product on “core defense requirements” by 2035, plus an additional 1.5 per cent of GDP for “defense and security-related spending.”

They specified that the aim is to “protect…critical infrastructure, defend … networks, ensure civil preparedness and resilience, unleash innovation, and strengthen [the] defense industrial base.” What they did not specify, however, was whether and how those funds would be spent in a manner that contributes most efficiently to the alliance’s common defense.

The allies’ commitment to increase their spending is certainly a welcome development. It results from a combination of increased fears of the Russian threat to Europe and President Trump’s threats to leave the allies to their own devices if they do not increase their defense budgets.

Nevertheless, European increases in spending will not necessarily result in commensurate increases in defense capability. The European NATO allies have been plagued by unnecessary duplication for decades. International rivalries, coupled with a longstanding determination  to protect their respective domestic industrial bases, have led member states to produce multiple versions of aircraft, ships and submarines, armor and other military equipment. As a result, the alliance is considerably less efficient than it otherwise might be.

Although NATO states have made some progress in rationalizing their domestic industrial bases they have by no means reached maximum efficiency. The latest example of the challenge to their ability to do so is, as has often been the case in the past, the difficulty of rationalizing aircraft production.

A team at the Financial Times reported last week that Italy had rebuffed a British effort to include German participation in the British-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Program to develop a sixth-generation fighter. The program represents a hedge against America backing away from Europe (and for that matter, East Asia); it would create an alternative to purchasing American aircraft.

The Financial Times reported that although Germany could make a major financial contribution to the project and increase orders for the plane, “officials from [Japan and Italy] … fear that their aerospace companies would lose work if German industrial players, including Airbus, joined the program.” Instead, the two partners were prepared to offer Germany the same “observer status,” they had granted to Canada — an offer Germany would certainly reject. 

The Germans had previously parted ways with France for joint development of another sixth-generation plane, “the Future Combat Air System.” Germany had pulled out of the project due to disagreements over who would lead it; how to distribute work share; and ultimately, over the plane’s mission. Paris wanted a smaller aircraft to fly off French aircraft carriers; Berlin wanted a larger plane for overland air superiority.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz seemed to go even further when he asked, “Will we still need a manned fighter jet in 20 years’ time … given that we will have to develop it at great expense?” Evidently, the Germans subsequently had second thoughts about remaining outside a European fighter program, but the distribution of workshare was another matter. 

The Italian government quickly rejected the Financial Times report. The Defense Ministry stated that it had offered Germany observer status “precisely to facilitate and accelerate this process…as an immediate facilitator of information-sharing on the program with a view to subsequent full membership.” The offer “was not intended to limit Germany’s future role in the program. On the contrary: it was aimed at accelerating the conditions for its involvement as much as possible, whilst safeguarding the program’s progress and the established timetable.”

Yet the Italian denial was not a complete denial. “Safeguarding the program’s progress and…timetable” could provide an excuse for excluding Germany if there was schedule slippage. Once again, industrial base issues appear to be complicating Europe’s effort not only to spend defense funds more efficiently, but to reduce its reliance on American military systems, despite the Trump administration‘s pressure on the allies to spend their defense funds on more purchases from U.S. contractors.

Programs such as Global Combat Air Program and the Future Combat Air System certainly represent a European hedge against a possible reduction of American support for NATO and reflect Europe’s growing desire to wean itself off American military sales. Yet the flap over German participation in the former, as well as Berlin’s break with Paris over the nature and management of the latter, highlights the challenges that continue to plague any European effort to develop a coherent and efficient industrial base. That goes not only for aircraft, but also for other key military capabilities they lack, such as airlift, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.

As long as the NATO allies cannot reorganize and rationalize their industrial production, they will find that they must still rely on purchases from American contractors, whether they like it or not. 

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Don Lemon gives condition for presidential bid
data.description:
Don Lemon, independent journalist and frequent critic of President Trump, said he would run for president if Democrats could reverse the Supreme Court decision that ushered dark money into politics. 

Lemon told podcast host David Siorta that he would “100 percent” launch a bid for the White House if Democrats could reverse the effects of the Citizens United decision of 2010. The ex-CNN anchor has recently floated the idea of running for president and said he has been frequently asked to run. 

“If the Democrats come in and they get rid of — or they do what they need to do with Citizens United — they take the money out of politics — I will say 100% I will run,” Lemon said. 

In Citizens United, the Supreme Court held that corporations have the same free speech rights that individuals do, allowing them to spend unlimited funds on campaign advertising as long as they don’t coordinate with candidates. In effect, the decision birthed super PACs, political action committees that can skirt disclosure requirements by taking money from opaque ‘dark money’ groups.

Citizens United is a common target of Democrats, who often decry the decision for corrupting the political system and allowing wealthy individuals to push millions of dollars into a race attempting to sway the election. Many Democrats refuse to take money from corporate PACs. 

Lemon said while he hasn’t aspired to be president, he would respond to a call to serve. 

“I think if we start having campaigns where the people show you if they want you or not through their donations and their support, then I will 100% do it, if they can get rid of it before it’s time for me to declare,” he said. 

Lemon said he frequently speaks to everyday people to understand the “pulse of what people are talking about.” He said that, plus the fact that he understands what it is like to be discriminated against as a Black, gay man, gives him the qualities needed to run for president. 

“It’s because I care about the American people,” Lemon said. “It’s because I can relate to the American people.”

data.title: Hawley says wife trying to discourage presidential campaign
data.description:
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) said he is giving “serious thought” to his role in Republican politics as the 2028 election cycle inches closer.

Hawley, in an interview with NBC News, said he was alarmed by the outcome of the midterms, when Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress, and wanted to do his part to help the GOP move forward.

“I was alarmed by the results of the election, and I’m concerned about the direction of both my party and the country,” the Missouri Republican told NBC on Thursday. “I’ve got four years here to serve in the Senate, and I’m just trying to think about where I am and what’s in front of me, what can I do to help the country go forward.”

As to whether Hawley — who has long been floated as a potential presidential contender — will stage a run for the White House, he told the outlet his wife has yet to be convinced. 

The senator was first elected to the upper chamber of Congress in 2019 and has been a key conservative voice ever since. But the Republican has at times pushed back against the Trump administration and GOP hard-liners, including calling for an end to the Iran War.

Hawley has also worked with progressives in an attempt to break up big medicine and push back on Wall Street. 

The midterm rout, he told NBC, sends a message to the GOP that it’s time to refocus on the working class and address high prices. The lawmaker said his party would continue to stand up for blue collar voters, even while in the minority.

“I think people are saying we want you to focus on us. Quit focusing on tech companies and data centers. Quit focusing on stuff overseas,” Hawley continued. “Focus on us. Do something to help us and our families. And that’s not too much to ask.”

The senator’s populist posture and desire to work across the aisle to deliver on certain policies — like eliminating taxes on healthcare, banning Flock cameras and capping the cost of prescription drugs — could give him a defined platform on which to run for president.

But it appears that before he can make a decision on a White House bid, he will first need to convince his wife. 

“Well, my wife is trying to discourage it,” he added.

data.title: Bolton: 'No substance' to Trump meeting with Putin, Xi
data.description:
Former White House national security adviser John Bolton said the trilateral meeting this week between President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping has “no substance.”

“I think from what we can tell of the trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi, there is no substance to it, whatever,” Bolton said in an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance.”

During the talks, which occurred on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China, the world leaders were expected to touch on trade, the wars in Ukraine and Iran and rapidly evolving artificial intelligence.

Trump also met individually with Xi and Putin.

“I think if there was any content, it came in the bilateral meetings earlier today of Putin with Trump and Xi with Trump,” Bolton told host Leland Vittert. “We’ll learn more, but overall, at this point, I would rate substance level pretty close to zero.”

The trio did issue a four-point “declaration toward peace.” The symbolic agreement says, “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” It also notes that the U.S., China and Russia will conduct a dialogue on “reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”

Bolton weighed in on the vow, saying “that was Ronald Reagan’s favorite line, so I’m happy to see that revived.”

Republican lawmakers have been divided on the trilateral talks, with some backing open conversations between the superpowers and others critical of the message the conversations send to Americans and others.

“I’ve never been successful in getting inside the president’s head, but I can tell you where I am, we have to be more clear about who our friends are and who our allies are,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said earlier this month. “I would put neither of those in that category.”

Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.), also a member of the panel, described Xi and Putin as “adversaries,” but noted that the president’s meeting with them was a “healthy thing.” 

Bolton said that while Trump considers Putin and Xi as friends, it probably does not go both ways.

“I will guarantee you, that’s not how they see him,” he added.

data.title: Burchett says you're a 'bad parent' if you let your child play 'GTA 6'
data.description:
GOP Rep. Tim Burchett (Tenn.) warned parents against allowing their children to play the new “Grand Theft Auto 6” video game amid its rollout this week. 

“These kids’ parents, are they wolves or something, raising their kids? I think it’s really just more of a how-to video,” the Tennessee Republican told TMZ on Wednesday, according to a video shared on social media by the entertainment news outlet. 

When asked by TMZ’s Jacob Wasserman about whether permitting children to play the game made someone a “bad parent,” Burchett replied, “I believe so.”

GTA 6 was released on Thursday after a 13-year wait from the last version of the video game. The game, which is rated for mature audiences, allows players to move freely around an open-world gaming experience. 

Fox News pundits raised concerns about the game’s display of graphic violence and sexual content, warning it could promote violence among children who played it. 

“Kids have these games, and what are you teaching them?” FOX 5 New York Anchor Rosanna Scotto said on Thursday’s “Outnumbered” show. “How to steal a car, how to shoot someone, how to do something illegal. And, I don’t know, does it destigmatize crime?”

Kayleigh McEnany, an “Outnumbered” host and former White House press secretary, said that her son “will be nowhere near anything like this while in my household.”

“This is almost the equivalent of giving them a gun, at an age where they don’t understand responsibility,” Paul Mauro, a Fox News contributor, said.

data.title: The smart fridge hacks show food security requires trade security
data.description:
A recent wave of cyberattacks across Europe has revealed vulnerabilities in the infrastructure that keeps food moving from farms to consumers. In October, hackers infiltrated the refrigeration systems of hundreds of French grocery stores. Within hours, the systems defrosted, reaching temperatures up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. The attack spoiled hundreds of pounds of food, and the affected companies reported losses of several million euros. By November, six additional European Union countries experienced near-identical incidents.

And so hackers can now threaten our food supply with a few keystrokes. But governments risk making matters worse if they impose cybersecurity rules that favor national solutions over interoperability, weakening the resilience of the very food supply chains they seek to protect.

The Pentagon has sounded the alarm, revealing that at least six U.S. military commissaries faced similar refrigeration outages in August. In both France and the U.S., the affected systems have been traced to the Danish company Danfoss, which claims that hackers capitalized on outdated legacy software systems.

Cybersecurity investigations reveal the relative ease by which these attacks were conducted. France’s Predicta Lab demonstrated that 2,752 Danfoss systems were accessible on the open internet. More concerningly, it took New York-based Claroty a mere 28 minutes and just $6 to identify two vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems using Anthropic’s Claude AI models.  

This is the iceberg for the agribusiness sector, which is increasingly reliant on smart devices, sometimes called the Internet of Things (IoT), ranging from autonomous farming equipment to advanced supply chain management systems. Their interconnectedness carries a greater riskof cyber disruption.  

Congress has acknowledged these risks. In January 2025, The Farm and Food Cybersecurity Act was introduced, directing the Department of Agriculture to evaluate vulnerabilities in food and agriculture infrastructure and coordinating annual crisis simulations with other federal agencies.

Those are sensible steps. The cybersecurity threat is real. But so, too, is the danger of Congress turning a shared security problem into a trade barrier. 

Governments may be tempted to require that every imported refrigeration controller, industrial sensor and logistics platform meet new national cybersecurity rules. The United States could adopt its own technical regulations and certification processes. The EU and other trading partners might take a different tack. 

In this scenario, a supplier selling the same refrigeration technology into five markets might have to maintain five compliance programs, undergo five assessments and produce five sets of documentation. Companies would face delayed equipment replacements, fewer suppliers and higher costs. Worse, manufacturers might divert resources from fixing vulnerabilities to satisfying different bureaucratic checklists. 

That is not supply chain resilience. It is regulatory fragmentation masquerading as security. 

This risk isn’t hypothetical. The EU’s Cyber Resilience Act already establishes cybersecurity standards, certification procedures and compliance obligations for connected products sold in Europe. These requirements serve legitimate security objectives, but they also create another layer of regulatory barriers for foreign manufacturers. Unless Washington and Brussels coordinate their approaches, manufacturers could face costly redundancies in certification requirements. 

By contrast, the IoT Cybersecurity Improvement Act of 2020, the closest U.S. equivalent to the Cyber Resilience Act, regulates those connected devices used exclusively by federal agencies, relying on procurement requirements, voluntary standards and sector specific regulation.

If the United States eventually moves toward more sweeping cybersecurity requirements, federal agencies must ensure cross-border compatibility for access controls, security updates, vulnerability disclosures and incident reporting. Where different systems achieve equivalent security outcomes, regulators should recognize that equivalence rather than insist on duplicative testing, including through mutual recognition agreements with trusted allies. The emphasis should be on performance over provenance. 

Internationally developed standards offer a useful starting point. The National Institute of Standards and Technology already provides a flexible cybersecurity framework, while industrial control standards can help manufacturers and operators address risks across borders. None of this requires relaxing protections. 

Governments must be free to exclude genuinely unsafe equipment or respond to specific national security threats. But requirements should target demonstrated vulnerabilities and should distinguish security benefits from preferences for domestic suppliers. 

Cybersecurity standards must also reflect the realities of American agriculture. Small family farms account for 86 percent of farms and 17 percent of the value of agricultural production. Many of these farms lack the resources to replace vulnerable equipment or hire cybersecurity specialists. 

To address this problem, the Cybersecurity in Agriculture Act would establish regional centers to develop security tools and train agricultural operators. Importantly, Congress should further ensure that equipment manufacturers shoulder responsibility for secure design and software updates.  

Washington has spent years warning that dependence on global supply chains creates vulnerabilities. But the answer is not to divide those supply chains into national silos. A fragmented regulatory system would limit businesses’ choices, access to secure technology and capacity to respond when disruptions occur. 

The refrigeration attacks are a wake-up call. Food security is trade security. Allied governments must strengthen cybersecurity without creating a patchwork of national rules that jeopardizes interoperability and leaves critical food supply chains more vulnerable.  

Ella Busch is a military operations analyst at Systems Planning & Analysis. Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University.

data.title: This Thanksgiving, be grateful for James Madison
data.description:
In both of his terms, and especially over the last two years, President Trump has stress-tested the Constitution in ways we didn’t imagine possible. But James Madison did.

There are a number of constitutional safeguards we have come to regard as quaint, or even obsolete, like the Third Amendment, forbidding the quartering of troops. But as Madison foresaw, these are now coming into their own, precisely when they are most needed.

Take the grand jury requirement in the Fifth Amendment. In 2016, federal prosecutors were unable to get grand juries to issue indictments only six times out of more than 150,000 attempts. But things are different now. Prosecutors might be able to get a grand jury to indict a ham sandwich, but not, as it turns out, a Subway sandwich.

One of the defining features of the Trump Department of Justice is its frequent grand jury face-plants. Time and time again, the Justice Department has sought to bring politically motivated cases designed to punish Trump’s enemies. And time and time again, grand juries have protected innocent people from the president’s wrath.

There’s Cassidy Hutchinson, who bravely testified about what happened at the White House on Jan. 6, 2021, during the Capitol Hill attacks. There is Letitia James, the state prosecutor who had the audacity to enforce her state’s elections laws, escaped indictment not once but twice for bogus charges of mortgage fraud. And let’s not forget the six members of Congress, all veterans, who made a video encouraging service members to follow the law and refuse illegal orders. That’s just a partial list.

It turns out we only thought the grand jury requirement was useless because it was working. Indictments were easy to get because prosecutors were rigorously ethical about only bringing cases they knew had merit. The minute U.S. attorneys began substituting politics for the rule of law, the grand jury came into its own and began doing what it was always intended to do: short-circuit efforts to use the justice system as a tool of oppression.

Madison was also way ahead of Trump when it comes to the latter’s efforts to intimidate the incoming Congress over its planned schedule of investigations into the last two years of White House sponsored legal and ethical mayhem.

It couldn’t be more clear that these efforts have everything to do with politics and nothing to do with justice. A letter filled with Native American stereotypes directed to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) by Aaron Reitz, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, ordered her to preserve documents and threatened her with sanctions if she didn’t. “You appear eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates,” he wrote. Similar, though slightly less cringe-inducing, letters were sent to Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

But thanks to Madison and the speech and debate clause that he wrote into the Constitution, this is all performative nonsense. The clause provides that, “for any Speech or Debate in either House, [members of Congress] shall not be questioned in any other Place.” This is, in effect, a grant of absolute immunity for anything that members of Congress do while engaging in legislative activities — that includes conducting congressional investigations. Warren is free to take her gavel and — metaphorically, of course — beat Trump and his “private associates” bloody with it. There is absolutely nothing Reitz, Blanche or anyone else can do about it — at least, not constitutionally.

Of course, you never know with Trump. But if there is one line he could cross that would convince a dozen Republican senators to vote for conviction in an impeachment trial, arresting members of Congress for doing their jobs is probably it.

This doesn’t mean that America’s constitutional government doesn’t need a lot of emergency repairs. You can’t see bits of it falling off yet, but the Supreme Court is now a zombie institution. It is impossible to confirm a new Supreme Court justice unless the same party controls both the presidency and the Senate. That means a court operating at less than full strength, possibly for years at a time, and wild ideological swings when the political stars align so that several Supreme Court seats can be filled at once.

And that’s just one example. We must fix the presidential immunity problem, take steps to clean up the presidential pardon system, shore up the independence of the Department of Justice, and make a host of other reforms. After 240 years, that’s no surprise. Madison and the founders couldn’t think of everything, and they couldn’t have anticipated the complexities of the modern world. There’s no denying that some of their solutions are more suited to the 18th century than the 21st.

There is a lot of work ahead of us, and we can take nothing for granted. But the founders had excellent instincts. Despite unprecedented effort to subvert it, the constitutional democracy they built still works. As we head into Thanksgiving, that’s something both Republicans and Democrats can be thankful for.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney and charter member of the Society for the Rule of Law.
